chapter_theme: Under the heading வெகுளாமை, nine verses on not answering provocation with anger: the great are not heated by the small, the man of unquenched anger is to be avoided, a feud dies as one tends one's own good, a mocking jest rebounds on the jester, the talk of strangers and the lies of the hired cannot be stopped and need not be grieved, the learned do not gore back the fool any more than one gores a cow, abuse returned sets one's own house on fire, and nobility comes from enduring rather than punishing.

51.reading: Even when the very small do them harm, those made excellent by birth weigh the matter and do not grow angry, for water heated however hot with good firewood never sets the house on fire.
51.nuance: The proverb grants that the great are heated, as water is by good fuel, and denies only that the heat does harm: water hot enough to scald still cannot burn the house that holds it. The verse grounds this restraint in birth (பிறப்பினால் மாண்டார்), not in learning or effort, and the counsel turns on திறத்துள்ளி, weighing the nature of the offender.

norm.note: a lineage claim of the period: freedom from anger is credited to those excellent by birth, set against the very small (இறப்பச் சிறியவர்)

pazhamozhi.proverb: நல்ல விறகின் அடினும் நனிவெந்நீர் இல்லம் சுடுகலா வாறு
pazhamozhi.literal: though heated with good firewood, very hot water cannot burn down the house

story.act: no story; the proverb is the household image of boiling water that scalds but cannot set its house alight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the well-born may be heated by the harm of small men but their heat does no damage

52.reading: A man whose anger never cools has no sense, and the wise say the best course is to keep out of his way, for it is hard to trust one who never becomes clear.
52.nuance: The counsel is not to bear the angry man but to step aside from him (மாறி ஒழுகல்), and the proverb gives the reason: one who never settles into clearness (தெளியான்) cannot be relied on. The address to the lord of the wave-beaten shore (சேர்ப்ப) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is hard to trust one who is not clear-minded

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of the man whose anger never subsides

pazhamozhi.applied_to: avoid the man of unquenchable anger, since he cannot be trusted

53.reading: The verse asks whether one must show force at everything that befalls one, and says that for the learned it is enough to guard themselves from anger, since as grass wears away when paddy is grown, a long enmity perishes of itself when one does one's own work.
53.nuance: The image makes the feud a weed that dies not by being pulled but by being crowded out by the crop: tending one's own field is the whole remedy. தற்செய்ய could also mean 'when one does good to oneself'; either way the action is on one's own side, not against the enemy.

pazhamozhi.literal: a long enmity perishes of itself when one does one's own part

story.act: no story; the proverb is set beside the farmer's sight of grass dying out as the paddy grows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned need not retaliate, since a feud starves when one simply tends one's own good

54.reading: Those at whom an unfit jest is aimed take it as abuse, so the jester is like the rat that carries off the lamp and brings harm on itself.
54.nuance: The verse comes at anger from the other side: the counsel is not to restrain one's own anger but not to rouse another's with a mocking word, which the hearer takes as reviling (வைதாரா). The rat that drags the lamp's wick sets fire to itself or its nest; the harm returns to the one who started it. Its place under வெகுளாமை rests on that reversal.

pazhamozhi.literal: a rat taking the lamp and causing harm to itself

story.act: a rat that seizes a burning lamp and is hurt by it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the one who makes an unfit jest draws the hearer's anger on himself

55.reading: When one hears the senseless words of those who do not understand, one should sit as if untouched, for those who try to stop the mouths of heartless strangers are like men who would lock up the public hall.
55.nuance: The reason given for silence is futility, not virtue: the hall (அம்பலம்) belongs to everyone and has no door to bolt, and the talk of strangers (வம்பலர்) is as open. பரியாதார் போல, 'as if not grieved', admits that the words do hurt and asks only that the hurt not be shown.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who would bar the public hall with a bolt

story.act: no story; the proverb names the absurd effort of locking a hall that stands open to all

pazhamozhi.applied_to: trying to silence the idle talk of strangers is futile, so one should sit unmoved

56.reading: If worthless men, having eaten their fill at the hands of one's enemies, speak lies about one for their sake, there is no cause for grief, the verse tells a woman, since what is charged is a thing one never did.
56.nuance: The slanderers are hirelings: கையார உண்டமையால் makes their lies a return for food given by those who bear a grudge (காய்வார்). The comfort rests on innocence alone; a true charge is left outside the counsel. The quoted words read as the end of a question (what grief is there, if it is said you did what you did not?), so the proverb is only a clause, and its sense depends on the words before it.

pazhamozhi.literal: if it is said one did what one did not do

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone falsely accused by men paid in food

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a false charge spread by hired slanderers is no cause for grief or anger

57.reading: The learned do not answer in heat the petty talk of those without examined knowledge, for no one gores back a cow that gores him.
57.nuance: The proverb ranks the unlearned speaker with a beast: the cow's butting is in its nature and returning it would make a man its equal. The image is a cow, not a hostile animal, so the fool's offence is treated as artless rather than wicked. The hill-country frame (honey licked by the monkey) is an address to the lord of the hills.

pazhamozhi.literal: if a cow gores, there are none who gore it back

story.act: no story; the proverb rests on the plain fact that no one butts back a cow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned do not retort to the empty words of the unlearned

58.reading: When those who cannot bear hurtful words revile in return with their tongue, the verse tells a woman, that abuse is the way of setting fire to one's own house.
58.nuance: The proverb is best read as தீ இல்லை ஊட்டும் திறம், 'the way of feeding fire to the house', so the retort burns the one who makes it. Line 2's வயவுரை is unclear; the reading takes it as the reviling word returned.

pazhamozhi.literal: the manner of setting fire to a house

story.act: no story; the proverb names arson against one's own dwelling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering abuse with abuse destroys the one who answers

59.reading: To bear with and go on past those who provoked one and did one harsh things is the way to renown, while punishing them brings no gain, since nobility comes only when one endures.
59.nuance: The verse sets two fruits apart: renown (புகழ்) from enduring, and nothing (பயனின்றே) from punishing, though it assumes the power to punish is there (ஒறுத்தாற்றின்). The proverb then names the deeper fruit, சால்பு, as something that arrives (வரும்) of itself to one who endures. சுறுத்தாற்றி in line 1 is a rare form; the reading takes it as 'provoking'.

pazhamozhi.literal: nobility comes when one oneself endures

story.act: no story; the proverb is a maxim about how worth is gained

pazhamozhi.applied_to: forbearing toward those who harmed one, not punishing them, yields renown and nobility

links.note: Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like heat taken on by boiled water; Pazhamozhi 51 uses the same heated water to say the well-born's heat, while it lasts, cannot burn the house.
links.teaches: Read together, the boiled-water image answers two questions: the Naladiyar says the worthy's anger does not last, Pazhamozhi says it does no harm even at its height.
links.list_adds: its proverb shifts the image from the cooling of the heat to the house that survives it, so harmlessness is added to brevity.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 51 credits freedom from anger to those excellent by birth (பிறப்பினால் மாண்டார்). The tension holds on reading பிறப்பு in 51 as lineage rather than nature.
links.teaches: The pair shows two accounts of where restraint comes from: the Kural makes worth follow what one does, while Pazhamozhi makes a virtue of conduct the mark of a good birth.
links.list_adds: it sets the great by birth against the very small and makes forbearance the sign that separates them, the ranking the couplet refuses.

links.note: Naladiyar 71 says to speak nothing to a fool and slip away; Pazhamozhi 52 gives the same withdrawal as the answer to a man of unquenchable anger and grounds it in his untrustworthiness.
links.teaches: Together they show that withdrawal, not endurance, is the counsel for two cases, the fool and the man of lasting anger, and Pazhamozhi supplies the reason: neither can be trusted with one's words.
links.list_adds: it carries the quatrain's withdrawal from the fool to the man of lasting anger and adds a proverb that names distrust as the ground.

links.note: Kural 510 warns against trusting one not examined; Pazhamozhi 52 names unquenchable anger as a sign that a man fails the test and is to be avoided.
links.teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general rule on examined trust into a usable test, since a man whose anger never cools shows by it that he is never clear and so not to be trusted.
links.list_adds: it names one observable trait, anger that never cools, as the mark of the untrustworthy that the couplet leaves unspecified.

links.note: Kural 158 says to defeat those who wrong one in excess by one's own fitness; Pazhamozhi 53 says the long feud dies of itself as grass does when paddy is grown.
links.teaches: The Kural states that rightness defeats excess and Pazhamozhi shows how: like a crop crowding out weeds, one's own good work starves the enmity without any act against the enemy.
links.list_adds: its farming proverb gives the mechanism, crowding out rather than fighting, that the couplet's language of victory leaves unstated.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and counts living so that enmity ends as good; Pazhamozhi 53 says how the enmity ends: by tending one's own good rather than by force.
links.teaches: The counted verse names ending a feud as a good to aim at, and Pazhamozhi shows that the aim is reached by not aiming at the enemy at all, since the feud withers on its own.

links.note: Kural 995 says scorn hurts even in jest; Pazhamozhi 54 adds that the hearer takes the jest as abuse and the harm returns on the jester, like a rat burnt by the lamp it seized.
links.teaches: The Kural looks at the pain a jest gives the hearer, Pazhamozhi at the anger it rouses and the cost to the jester, so together they show a mocking word wounding both ends.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's concern for the hearer into a warning about self-harm, the rat burnt by its own theft.

links.note: Naladiyar 72 bids silence before the unfit words of those not one's equals because the world counts a retort as disgrace; Pazhamozhi 55 bids the same silence because silencing strangers is as futile as bolting a public hall.
links.teaches: The pair gives two different grounds for one silence, reputation in the Naladiyar and futility in Pazhamozhi, which shows the counsel can rest on prudence alone without appeal to honour.
links.list_adds: its proverb replaces the quatrain's appeal to the world's judgement with the plain impossibility of shutting an open hall.

links.note: Kural 185 says backbiting exposes the meanness of the backbiter; Pazhamozhi 56 says the target of hired lies has no cause for grief, since the charge is false.
links.teaches: Held together, the two verses show slander's weight falling wholly on the speaker: the Kural says it exposes him, Pazhamozhi that it leaves the innocent target nothing to grieve.
links.list_adds: it adds the slanderer's motive, food from one's enemies, and the victim's side, which the couplet on the backbiter does not consider.

links.note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bites back a raging dog; Pazhamozhi 57 says no one gores back a cow. Both make a beast of the insulter to show that retaliation is beneath a person.
links.teaches: The two images differ in what they make of the insulter: the Naladiyar's biting dog is vicious, Pazhamozhi's goring cow is merely artless, so the unlearned are excused where the low are condemned.
links.list_adds: it puts a cow in the dog's place and the unlearned in the place of the low, softening the judgement on the offender.

links.note: Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths; Pazhamozhi 57 says the learned do not retort to the unlearned, for no one gores back a cow.
links.teaches: The Kural calls forbearance toward fools a strength, and Pazhamozhi gives the ground of that strength: a learned man who retorts makes himself the equal of an animal, so restraint keeps the rank between them.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes the fool a beast whose offence cannot be returned, a ranking the couplet's paradox of strength does not draw.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 51 says the well-born's heat, like hot water, cannot burn the house; 58 says that abuse returned is the very act of setting the house on fire.
links.teaches: Read side by side, the two verses draw the line between heat felt and heat spoken: anger held inside does no harm, while anger turned into a retort burns down one's own house.

links.note: Naladiyar 63 says unguarded words burn the speaker without end; Pazhamozhi 58 says returned abuse sets fire to one's own house.
links.teaches: Both place the burn of an angry word on the speaker, and Pazhamozhi widens it from the speaker's self to his household, the house as the thing consumed.
links.list_adds: its proverb names the house, not the speaker's mind, as what the retort burns, widening the harm beyond the self.

links.note: Kural 987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm; Pazhamozhi 59 says worth (சால்பு) comes from enduring such people rather than punishing them.
links.teaches: The pair sets two thresholds for nobility: Pazhamozhi grants சால்பு to one who merely endures the wrongdoer, while the Kural asks that the wrongdoer also be done good.
links.list_adds: it sets enduring against punishing and gives each its fruit, renown against nothing, where the couplet asks a third thing, doing good.

links.note: Naladiyar 65 says true patience is that of the strong who could punish all; Pazhamozhi 59 says punishing those who harmed one, though one could, brings no gain.
links.teaches: Both assume the power to punish, and together they show that forbearance counts as a virtue only when retaliation is open, and then gains what punishment cannot.
links.list_adds: it adds the outcome of the forgone punishment, no gain, and of the forbearance, renown and nobility, to the quatrain's test of strength.

source_issues: 56: the quotation marks enclose only செய்யாத செய்தா வெனில், the end of a question begun by என்பரிவ; the proverb may properly include the question word.
58 line 2: வயவுரை is obscure and may be a copying error (perhaps for வசையுரை); line 4 is best divided தீ இல்லை ஊட்டும் திறம்.
59 line 1: சுறுத்தாற்றி is a rare form whose sense (provoking) is inferred from context.
